summary: This assessment explores the complex interactions between human and climatic drivers of desertification, the challenges in mapping and quantifying desertification, and the feedback mechanisms between desertification and climate, including sand/dust aerosols, albedo changes, and greenhouse gas fluxes.

heading_path: 3.1.4.3 Interaction of drivers: Desertification syndrome versus drylands development paradigm
passages.text: All in all, there is high confidence that anthropogenic and climatic drivers interact in complex ways in causing desertification. As discussed in Section 3.2.2, the relative influence of human or climatic drivers on desertification varies from place to place (high confidence).

heading_path: 3.2 Observations of desertification
3.2.1 Status and trends of desertification
passages.text: Depending on the definitions applied and methodologies used in evaluation, the status and extent of desertification globally and regionally still show substantial variations (high confidence). There is high confidence that the range and intensity of desertification has increased in some dryland areas over the past several decades.

heading_path: 3.3 Desertification feedbacks to climate
passages.text: Drylands are characterised by limited soil moisture compared to humid regions. Thus, the sensible heat (heat that causes the atmospheric temperature to rise) accounts for more of the surface net radiation than latent heat (evaporation) in these regions. This tight coupling between the surface energy balance and the soil moisture in semi-arid and dry sub-humid zones makes these regions susceptible to land–atmosphere feedback loops that can amplify changes to the water cycle.

heading_path: 3.3 Desertification feedbacks to climate
3.3.1 Sand and dust aerosols
passages.text: Biological or structural soil crusts have been shown to effectively stabilise dryland soils. Thus their loss due to intense land use and/or climate change can be expected to cause an increase in sand and dust storms (high confidence).

heading_path: 3.3 Desertification feedbacks to climate
3.3.1 Sand and dust aerosols
passages.text: There is high confidence that there is a negative relationship between vegetation green-up and the occurrence of dust storms. Changes in groundwater can affect vegetation and the generation of atmospheric dust. This can occur through groundwater processes such as the vertical movement of salt to the surface causing salinisation, supply of near-surface soil moisture, and sustenance of groundwater dependent vegetation.

heading_path: 3.3 Desertification feedbacks to climate
3.3.2 Changes in surface albedo
passages.text: Increasing surface albedo in dryland regions will impact the local climate, decreasing surface temperature and precipitation, and provide a positive feedback on the albedo (high confidence).

heading_path: 3.3 Desertification feedbacks to climate
3.3.3 Changes in vegetation and greenhouse gas fluxes
passages.text: Desertification usually leads to a loss in productivity and a decline in above- and below-ground carbon stocks. Drivers such as overgrazing lead to a decrease in both plant and SOC pools.

heading_path: 3.4 Desertification impacts on natural and socio-economic systems under climate change
3.4.1 Impacts on natural and managed ecosystems
3.4.1.1 Impacts on ecosystems and their services in drylands
passages.text: There is high confidence that desertification processes such as soil erosion, secondary salinisation, and overgrazing have negatively impacted provisioning ecosystem services in drylands, particularly food and fodder production.

heading_path: 3.4 Desertification impacts on natural and socio-economic systems under climate change
3.4.1 Impacts on natural and managed ecosystems
3.4.1.1 Impacts on ecosystems and their services in drylands
passages.text: Precipitation, by affecting soil moisture content, is considered to be the principal determinant of the capacity of drylands to sequester carbon. Lower annual rainfall resulted in the release of carbon into the atmosphere for a number of sites located in Mongolia, China and North America. Low soil water availability promotes soil microbial respiration, yet there is insufficient moisture to stimulate plant productivity, resulting in net carbon emissions at an ecosystem level.

heading_path: 3.4 Desertification impacts on natural and socio-economic systems under climate change
3.4.1 Impacts on natural and managed ecosystems
3.4.1.2 Impacts on biodiversity: Plant and wildlife
passages.text: Desertification, including through land-use change, already contributed to the loss of biodiversity across drylands (medium confidence).
